# Agent Instructions


## Project Wiki Conventions

A git-tracked, agent-readable knowledge base for non-technical project context (domain, product, design, engineering, operations, gtm, governance). Opt-in per project; disabled when the `wiki` config group is absent.

**REQUIRED:** read `wiki-federation-model` (three-layer model, federation table, origination modes, authorship hedges), `wiki-conventions` (cross-reference protocol, before resolving a link), `wiki-page-spec` (before interpreting or validating a page's frontmatter), `wiki-page-types` (page types with their authorship and freshness defaults and per-type required fields), `wiki-configuration` (where the wiki and its reports are), `wiki-page-freshness` (before interpreting freshness behavior), and `wiki-tree-layout` (before enumerating or walking a sub-wiki's pages).
**REQUIRED:** read `wiki-write-protocol` (authorship boundary, v1 deferrals) and `wiki-authoring-spec` (the readability rules and the list of every author-facing lookup, all materialized into the wiki at `_authoring/`); read `wiki-page-spec` also before authoring a page, `wiki-page-slugs` before deriving a filename from a title, and `wiki-configuration` before `/wiki-init`.


## Project-Specific Instructions

### Sundal

Sundal is a mobile-first app that lets snack shop vendors manage stock, see what each company's employees have bought from the shop, and see the monthly total each company owes. Employees record their own purchases at the shop.

#### Users

- **Vendor:** runs the shop from a phone and has very little time to spare. Sets snack prices and stock levels, serves multiple companies, and can void a single entry, meaning one snack line of a purchase.
- **Employee:** works at a company the vendor serves and uses a phone at the shop. Has one personal sign-in, active on one phone at a time, and records only their own purchases by adding snacks to a purchase cart, reviewing the total, and recording it. Each snack line becomes its own entry. Cannot cancel an entry.
- **Company admin:** uses a phone. Sees the monthly total the company owes, as cumulative totals only, never who bought what.

#### Product rules

- Each company's purchases are totalled per month. The month closes automatically at midnight Indian time on its last day, and a closed month never changes. A void of an entry in a closed month appears in the open month as a labeled line.
- Each purchase keeps the price shown when it was made.
- The vendor builds the catalog: creates a category and names it, then adds items to it. Each item has a name, an image, a description, a stock quantity, and a price per item. Categories hold items directly, with no subcategories.
- Employees never see the stock number. Recording a purchase takes its quantity out of stock, and an employee cannot add more of an item than its stock allows; an item at zero shows "Out of stock". Voiding an entry returns its quantity to stock. Only the vendor changes stock counts directly.
- The employee's purchase cart is kept on their account until they record it or empty it, and shows the same items at the next sign-in. The cart bar is hidden while the cart is empty.
- Employees change quantity with + and − buttons only, one per tap, with no typing and no repeat on hold. The vendor's stock quantity is a number field with + and − buttons.
- Walk-in cash sales happen outside the app and are not recorded, so stock levels the vendor maintains can drift from the shelf.
- Payment features are V2 scope: marking a month as paid, the vendor raising an invoice, and the company paying in the app.

#### Constraints

- English only, built for all of India.
- Vendors, employees, and company admins use phones only.
- Online only: every app screen needs an internet connection. A purchase exists only once the server has confirmed it, and retrying the same confirm never records it twice.
- Offline behavior in the employee mobile app: when the phone goes offline, a toast says "You're offline" and nothing else on screen changes. When the employee taps anything that needs the server while offline, the screen shows "You're offline" with a Retry button, and nothing changes on the server. This applies to every action in the app.
- Preferences: simple for non-technical users, light on data, quick to ship.

#### Design references

- Blinkit, Zepto, and Instamart are the references for information architecture, UX patterns, and components.
- Sundal has no cart, payment, or delivery, and each entry holds one snack, so a borrowed pattern is adapted to those rules.

#### Scope boundaries

- Work is on UX screens. Technology choice is out of scope.
- The employee mobile app comes first.
- The wiki is built once the product is understood.

<!-- end-project-specific -->

## Plan Before Action Gate

**Predecessors:** `brainstorm` (when intent is unclear), `scope-work` (when intent is clear but delivery cost is not)
**Successors (REQUIRED):** `plan-before-action`
**Successors (REQUIRED):** `plan-execution-gate`

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER modify project artifacts in a way that changes behavior without first presenting a plan and obtaining approval to proceed. No exceptions.
</HARD-GATE>

### When to Apply
Whenever a task will modify project artifacts in a way that changes behavior or output — no matter how small, obvious, or quick the change seems.

Does NOT apply to:
- Read-only exploration
- Documentation-only changes — prose nothing runs or loads as instructions (READMEs, guides, code comments)
- Routine operations on already-decided work (commits, status updates)

The planning procedure that follows from this gate — tier determination, persistence, and the plan-review ask — lives in the `plan-before-action` workflow.

### Red Flags — STOP
If you catch yourself thinking any of these, stop — you are rationalizing:

- "This is just a one-line fix" -- still needs a structured plan and approval.
- "I already know what to do" -- knowing is not the same as having approval.
- "This is a follow-up to approved work" -- each task gets its own plan.
- "I'll just remember to write it down later." -- later is the next session, where you won't.

## Plan Execution Gate

**Predecessors (REQUIRED):** `plan-before-action-gate`
**Successors (REQUIRED):** `plan-execution`
**Successors (REQUIRED):** `git` — for the commit gate.
**Successors (REQUIRED):** `pr` — for the end-of-execution ask's PR answer.

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER deviate from an approved plan without stopping and obtaining approval to proceed first.
</HARD-GATE>

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER claim execution complete without running `check` against the diff first.
</HARD-GATE>

**See also:** `verification-before-completion` — for the evidence-pairings gate that backs the "verification was run" half.

### When to Apply
This applies after a plan (structured or full design doc) has been approved.

This does NOT apply to:
- Documentation-only changes
- Routine operations on already-decided work

### Red Flags — STOP
If you catch yourself thinking any of these, stop — you are rationalizing:

- "I'll just fix this one extra thing" -- not in the plan, don't touch it.
- "This is close enough to the plan" -- close is not the same, stop and ask.
- "I'll commit now and review later" -- review before commit, always.
- "The tests pass so it's fine" -- passing tests don't replace the review `check` runs.


### Plan Execution Gate (Design)

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER pass `check`'s quality review on a diff that changes a design page or UI source — code that renders what users see — without running `design-review` on it.
</HARD-GATE>

#### Design pages
A design page is a wiki page whose `<sub-wiki>:<type>` key, with the sub-wiki taken from its path and the type from its frontmatter, appears in `.agent-kit/dist/wiki/scripts/data/page-standards.json`, the file `content-review` reads for a page's governing standards. A page of a type no design standard governs is not a design page, wherever it lives. A build that deploys no such file has no design page.

#### Check augmentation
For the quality-review step: invoke the `design-review` skill on the design pages and UI source in the diff.

## Naming

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER create, rename, or move a file or folder without first checking its name against naming conventions.
</HARD-GATE>

### When to Apply
- Creating, renaming, or moving a file or folder.
- Creating a new repository.
- Approving a plan that introduces files.

Applies to all repositories — apps, services, libraries, infrastructure, docs.

**REQUIRED:** read `file-naming-patterns` — repository names, file and folder patterns, and anti-patterns.

**Defaults:** kebab-case file and folder names. No underscores. Numeric prefix (`NN-topic.ext`) only when intrinsic ordering or sequence identity applies. Source files follow language-pack rules (not this convention). Tool-mandated names (`README.md`, `package.json`, etc.) are exempt.

### Red Flags — STOP
- "I'll just use an underscore here" — consistency matters.
- "This file has no obvious group, let me invent one" — single-topic files don't need a forced prefix.
- "Numeric prefix will solve grouping" — a numeric prefix encodes reading order or sequence identity, not grouping; cluster with a shared prefix or a directory instead.
- "Tool requires this exact filename" — tool-mandated names are explicit exceptions, no issue.

## Durable Content

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER write content describing an enumerable list's cardinality, a fact that has one canonical home elsewhere, a review/execution moment, or a subject's relative recency without first checking it against durable-content patterns.
</HARD-GATE>

### When to Apply
- Writing or editing a rule, workflow, lookup, template, doc, wiki page, code comment, or commit/PR body.
- Describing an enumerable list (types, steps, schemas, checks) in prose.
- Citing a fact, count, or name that already lives somewhere else.
- Naming something by the review/execution round that produced it, or by its relative recency.

Applies to all repositories — docs, code comments, commit/PR bodies, wiki pages.

**REQUIRED:** read `durable-content-patterns` — the anti-pattern families, the discriminating tests, and worked before/after rewrites.

**Defaults:** describe the subject as it stands today, not the process, moment, or count that produced it. Let an enumerable list self-count instead of restating its cardinality in prose — this applies even when the count is the artifact's own designed structure (a playbook's stage count, a plugin's schema count), not only to lists that change often. State a fact once, at its one canonical location, and point to it elsewhere. Use a phase/stage label only when it names a position in a currently-documented, stable model — never a one-off review/execution round.

### Red Flags — STOP
- "Three transformations applied to..." — a prose number describing a list's current size; it will be wrong the next time the list changes, even if it's correct today.
- "Phase J", "Stage G", "revised per round 3" — a label that only resolves by knowing which now-closed session produced it.
- Restating a count, list, or name that already exists elsewhere in the same file or a sibling file, instead of pointing to it.
- "new", "recently added", "now supports", "currently" — describes a past-to-present transition rather than the subject's current behavior; misleading the moment something newer exists.

## Version Control

**Predecessors:** `plan-execution` (commit happens at end of execution)

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER commit directly to master. All work happens on prefixed branches.
</HARD-GATE>

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER force-push master without explicit approval to proceed.
</HARD-GATE>

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER run `git commit` without first invoking the `/git` skill.
</HARD-GATE>



### When to Apply
Whenever you are about to draft, suggest, or run a commit message; about to run `git rebase`, `git merge`, or `git push`; about to draft or edit a PR title or description; or about to create or suggest a branch name.

### Red Flags — STOP
If you catch yourself doing or thinking any of these, stop and correct:

- About to commit on master.
- Commit message has a body.
- Commit message ends with `Co-Authored-By:` or `Signed-off-by:`.
- PR title or body carries a trailer or attribution footer — `Co-Authored-By:`, `Signed-off-by:`, or a "Generated with …" line.
- Subject names the workflow ("Phase X", ticket reference, "addressed review findings") instead of the change itself.
- About to run `git push --force` (or `--force-with-lease`) on master without explicit approval to proceed.

## Verification Before Completion

**See also:** `plan-execution` — for the broader plan-execution lifecycle this rule fits into.

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER claim work is complete, fixed, or passing without running the relevant verification command and reading its output first.
</HARD-GATE>


### When This Applies
Any time you're about to:

- Claim an automated check passed, a defect is fixed, or work is complete
- Express satisfaction ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!")
- Commit, push, or open a PR
- Mark a task complete, move to the next task, or trust another agent's "success" report

### The Gate Function
Before any completion claim:

1. **IDENTIFY** — what command proves this claim?
2. **RUN** — execute the full command fresh against the current state (not a previous run, not a remembered result)
3. **READ** — full output, check exit code, count failures
4. **VERIFY** — does the output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: state actual status with evidence
   - If YES: state claim WITH evidence
5. **ONLY THEN** — make the claim

Skipping any step = lying, not verifying.

### Required Evidence by Claim Type
**REQUIRED:** read `verification-evidence` before any completion claim — it carries the claim-to-evidence pairings and the default for claim types its table does not list.

### Red Flags — STOP
If you catch yourself thinking any of these, stop — you're rationalizing:

- "Should work now", "Probably passes", "Seems fine" — hedge words are tells. Run the command, read the output, then claim.
- "The other check passed, so this one has" — one check passing is no evidence for another. Each claim has its own evidence.
- "Agent reported success, must be done" — verify the diff or the cited evidence yourself; another agent's self-report is not evidence.
- "Partial check is enough" — partial evidence is no evidence. Run the full command.
- "I'll verify after the commit" — commit IS a completion claim. Verify first.

## Read-Only Zones

<HARD-GATE>
NEVER create, modify, or delete files marked `AGENT-READONLY:` in their first 5 body lines, or files inside `.agent-kit/dist/**`, `.agent-kit/state/**`, or `.agent-kit/cache/**`.
</HARD-GATE>

The upstream `agent-kit` repo is maintained separately and is **not present in this project tree**. Fixes happen there and are re-deployed — never in the consuming project.

### When to Apply
Before any create, modify, or delete on a file marked `AGENT-READONLY:` in its first 5 body lines, on generated or deployed output, or on anything under `.agent-kit/dist/`, `.agent-kit/state/`, or `.agent-kit/cache/`.

### Deployed (Read-Only) Content
You MUST NOT create, modify, or delete:

- Your main agent-config file: `CLAUDE.md`
- Any skill, instruction, or rule file your provider reads from a directory adjacent to `CLAUDE.md`.
- **Any file containing the marker `AGENT-READONLY:` within its first 5 body lines** — this marker is the authoritative signal. *Body lines* are counted from the start of the body: line 1 of a file with no frontmatter, and the line after the closing `---` otherwise. The window is measured there because that is where the deploy writes the marker, so a file whose frontmatter runs past four lines still carries it.
- **Deploy-output namespace** (`.agent-kit/dist/**`), **deploy-managed runtime state** (`.agent-kit/state/**`), and **provisioned cache** (`.agent-kit/cache/**`) — never edit in place.

**REQUIRED:** read `deployed-paths-and-protocol` — deploy sub-tree details, editable paths catalog, and the conflict protocol for defects in read-only files.


### Red Flags — STOP
If you catch yourself thinking any of these, stop -- you are rationalizing:

- "It's just a typo, I'll fix it quickly" -- deploy-side fix, always.
- "This is clearly wrong, no need to ask" -- ask anyway, that is the protocol.
- "The marker isn't there so it must be editable" -- if it looks generated, verify before touching it.
- "Only frontmatter in the first 5 lines" -- look below the closing `---`; the window starts at the body.

## Behavioral Core

These defaults hold on every turn; a gate, a skill or the deployment's operating-mode contract that speaks to the situation governs it.

- **Claims and evidence:** Verify a claim about files, code or behavior by reading it now; a report, a plan's description of current state or an earlier run is a claim, not evidence.
- **Claims and evidence:** Never let "no findings" and "never checked" look alike: name what you skipped or dropped, and report a finding you disagree with, with why.
- **Feedback and review:** Treat feedback as a suggestion to evaluate, not an order: restate each item in your own words, verify it against the artifact, and clarify every unclear item before changing anything.
- **Feedback and review:** Show you heard it through the edit or a reasoned pushback, never agreement or praise; push back when a finding misreads the artifact, expands scope, is technically wrong or conflicts with a prior decision.
- **Feedback and review:** In a review, make each finding specific and actionable, suggest an alternative where you ask for a change, and report a clean result as clean instead of inventing problems.
- **Uncertainty:** When you do not know, say so and ask; do not guess or pretend.
- **Scope:** Hold to the stated goal: improve the work you are already in where that serves it, and give unrelated rework its own goal.
- **Scope:** Do not drift toward a more interesting problem or widen scope on a reviewer's suggestion; surface any redefinition of the goal explicitly.
- **Prose:** Write in active voice, cut hedges and filler, say each thing once and use one canonical term per concept; if a claim needs softening, fix the claim.
- **Prose:** Use the reader's vocabulary; define or drop internal jargon.
- **Questions and decisions:** Ask one question per turn with your recommended answer, and read the material before asking what it already answers; one extra question costs little and a wrong assumption compounds.
- **Questions and decisions:** Hard constraints exclude options and preferences only rank them; "there is only one way" means the alternatives were not considered.
- **Blockers and refusals:** When blocked, name the exact check, command or input that unblocks you and stop rather than guess.
- **Blockers and refusals:** A refusal from a tool, check, hook or permission is a finding to surface, never an obstacle to route around — by hand edits, skipped hooks, overrides or self-approval — unless the person explicitly authorizes that action.
- **Inference, orientation and handoff:** State an inferred value where the person can see it before you act on it, and when asked what is next give one prioritized step, not every gap.
- **Inference, orientation and handoff:** When orienting or teaching, stay one layer up in the project's own vocabulary, ground each claim in the source cited by path, and check understanding with something concrete.
- **Inference, orientation and handoff:** End a handoff on a concrete next action, not a status.
- **Sourcing:** Trace every claim to a source and say what each contributed; when sources disagree show both rather than silently picking one, and keep first-party sources distinct from derived syntheses.
- **Sourcing:** Say "no source covers this" instead of padding, and drop a citation that does not hold: it reads as coverage and hides the gap.
- **Destructive operations:** Before a destructive or irreversible operation, get explicit, specific confirmation; a plain yes does not count.

## Auto-Stop Signals

If the person says any of these, stop the current track immediately and ask before continuing:

| Phrase | What it means |
|--------|---------------|
| "we're mixing X" / "too many things" / "this is too broad" | Scope drift. The current plan or task bundles unrelated work. Stop and re-scope to a single thesis before continuing. |
| "shouldn't we X first" / "isn't X a precondition" | Ordering / dependency mistake. The current step assumes work that hasn't landed yet. Stop and either land the dependency or re-sequence. |
| "are we stuck?" | The current approach isn't progressing. Discuss the architectural choice, not the next fix. |
| "investigate" / "investigate first" | Don't propose solutions yet. Trace data and read the source. |
| "wait" / "hold on with the implementation" | Pause — alignment isn't reached yet. Don't jump from discussion to implementation. |
| "commit messages have ticket/phase refs" / "commit messages aren't following /git guidelines" / "review and update the commit messages" | Commit subject(s) failed the Commit Message Gate — workflow context (ticket, phase, sprint, review framing) leaked into the subject, or another `/git` rule was missed. Re-read the gate, rewrite each subject to describe the change itself; branch and PR carry workflow context. |

These are redirect phrases observed in person-to-agent corrections. Treat each as a hard stop and ask before continuing.

**All HARD-GATE blocks above:** violating the letter is violating the spirit.
